title: Nothing edited out
hookLine: the Gurus kept these voices and sometimes answered them in hymns of their own

lines: DELETE IT, OR COMMENT BESIDE IT?
cards: A shared document, the kind a team writes together. One person types a paragraph. Someone else disagrees.
They could delete it and write their own, or leave a comment in the margin: here's how I'd put it. The paragraph stays, the comment sits beside it, and anyone who opens the file later sees both.
The Guru Granth Sahib does something like that with the Bhagats, and it keeps both names on the page.

teach.h: THE BHAGATS, UNDER THEIR OWN NAMES.
teach.b: For weeks this path has walked through the Bhagats: Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas, Farid, Ramanand, Jaidev and more. Their words sit in the Granth under their own names.

And sometimes, right beside a Bhagat's verse, stands a verse marked with a Guru's name. It happens among Kabir's saloks, and among Farid's, and readers hear some of these as replies. Take one pair, on Ang 1380.
Farid says, in paraphrase: cut open my body and not a drop of blood comes out; those steeped in the Lord have no blood left.
Right after it, a verse marked with Guru Amar Das's number answers: this body is all blood, and without blood there is no body; what drains from one steeped in the Lord is the blood of greed.
Same image, carried a step further. The compilers had an easy move: cut a line a Guru would put differently, or smooth it into the Gurus' own voice. The Granth doesn't.

teach.h: A GURU'S VERSE BESIDE A BHAGAT'S.
teach.b: The Bhagat's words keep the Bhagat's name and way of saying it, and the Guru's verse comes in beside it, with the Guru's name.

teach.h: NOT CUT OR SMOOTHED: BOTH VISIBLE.
teach.b: A reader gets the conversation, not just the conclusion.

teach.h: A THIRD ROAD: KEEP IT WHOLE, THEN REPLY.
teach.b: So the Granth isn't one voice talking to itself. It's a house with many speakers, where the Gurus' voice leads and others are honored at the table, by name. And it offers a pattern for ordinary life.
When someone says a thing you'd say differently, there are two easy roads: pretend they never said it, or shout it down.
The Granth shows a third: keep their words whole, then answer beside them, in your own voice.

how: In the Guru Granth Sahib the Bhagats' compositions appear under their own names, and Sikh teachers point out the places where a Guru's salok stands beside a Bhagat's and takes up its theme.

o: the wanting-more that drains from the devoted
contentment with what one already has
anger, the fire that burns in a proud heart

games.q: how the Granth keeps voices — tap the pairs.
p: kept under the Bhagat's own name
read by some as a reply
cut it or smooth it over

s: the Bhagats' words were rewritten in the Gurus' voice
they keep the Bhagats' names and their own way of saying things.
among Kabir's and Farid's saloks there are verses marked with Gurus' names
readers hear some of them as replies.
the Granth records only one voice
it's a house of many speakers, the Gurus' voice leading and others named at the table.

games.q: you're compiling a holy book. a poet you honor has a line you'd put differently. what do you do?
o: rewrite it in your own words.
keep it whole and set your answer beside it.
games.why: the Granth keeps the Bhagat's words under the Bhagat's name, and at times a Guru's verse stands beside them as a reply.

practice: Think of someone who said something recently that you'd put differently, and let their words stand in your mind, whole, without trimming them to make them easier to dismiss.
Then shape your reply, not a correction shouted over them but a sentence beside theirs, and hold it until it's kind. If you pray, breathe out Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Greed. What Guru Amar Das names the blood that drains from one steeped in the Lord, answering Farid's verse beside it instead of erasing it.

carryVoice: Your line: answer, don't erase. Both voices can stay on the page, side by side. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Salok Farid 51 and Mahala 3 after it, Ang 1380
